papers.title: SpaCoEx: Sparse Gene Selection for Spatially Varying Co-expression in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: SpaCoEx is a computational method designed to identify pairs or groups of genes whose co-expression patterns vary meaningfully across space in spatial transcriptomics data. It uses sparse selection techniques to filter out noise and highlight only the most spatially informative gene relationships, rather than treating all genes uniformly. This helps researchers pinpoint localized gene interaction patterns that might reflect distinct cell states or microenvironments within tissue.
papers.why: This tool could help reveal spatially restricted co-expression modules relevant to interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net-associated gene programs within spatial transcriptomics datasets, potentially linking region-specific autophagy/mitophagy gene networks to their tissue context.

papers.title: AMPKα1 activation enhances mitophagy to counteract hypoxia-induced neuronal apoptosis in cervical spondylotic myelopathy and facilitates functional recovery mediated by rosmarinic acid.
papers.summary: This study investigates how rosmarinic acid, a natural compound, activates AMPKα1 to boost mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) in neurons under low-oxygen conditions. The researchers show this process helps prevent neuronal cell death in a model of cervical spondylotic myelopathy, a spinal cord compression disorder. Enhanced mitophagy through AMPKα1 signaling ultimately supported better functional recovery in the disease model.
papers.why: This paper's focus on AMPKα1-driven mitophagy protecting neurons from hypoxic apoptosis provides relevant mechanistic insight into mitophagy pathways in neurons, directly relevant to the PhD project's core theme even though it centers on spinal cord rather than brain interneurons or spatial omics methods.

papers.title: Deubiquitinases in mitophagy: therapeutic control of mitochondrial quality.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) regulate mitophagy, the process by which damaged mitochondria are tagged and selectively degraded. DUBs work opposite to ubiquitin ligases like Parkin, removing ubiquitin marks from mitochondrial proteins to fine-tune whether a mitochondrion is targeted for destruction. The abstract suggests these enzymes represent potential drug targets for controlling mitochondrial quality control in disease contexts.
papers.why: Since mitophagy in neurons is a core focus of the PhD project, understanding the ubiquitin-based regulatory machinery controlling mitochondrial degradation could inform mechanistic interpretation of spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic changes linked to neuronal mitochondrial quality control.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Crossroads in Neurobiology: From Cellular Vulnerability to Therapeutic Opportunity.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitochondria influence neuronal health, focusing on their role in energy production, calcium handling, and cell death pathways in the brain. It likely discusses how mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to neuronal vulnerability in aging and disease, and explores emerging therapeutic strategies targeting mitochondrial pathways. As a review-style piece, it probably synthesizes current understanding of mitochondrial biology relevant to neurodegeneration and brain function without presenting new experimental data.
papers.why: Understanding mitochondrial vulnerability and quality control mechanisms in neurons provides essential context for mitophagy and autophagy research in interneurons and perineuronal net-associated circuits.

papers.title: Mitochondrial homeodynamics in ageing: mechanisms, resilience, and interventions.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how mitochondria maintain a dynamic balance of quality control, biogenesis, and degradation—called homeodynamics—as organisms age. It discusses the mechanisms that break down during ageing, leading to accumulation of damaged mitochondria and reduced cellular resilience. The paper also covers potential interventions, such as boosting mitophagy or metabolic pathways, to restore mitochondrial balance and healthy ageing.
papers.why: Understanding mitochondrial quality control mechanisms and their decline with age is directly relevant to studying mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, particularly given the vulnerability of interneurons to metabolic and mitochondrial stress over the lifespan.

papers.title: Neuroglobin positively regulates YTHDF3 to restore mitophagy and suppress ferroptosis in sevoflurane-induced developmental neurotoxicity.
papers.summary: This study investigates how sevoflurane, a common anesthetic, causes neurotoxicity in the developing brain by disrupting mitophagy (the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria) and triggering ferroptosis (iron-dependent cell death). The researchers found that Neuroglobin, an oxygen-binding protein, can boost the activity of YTHDF3, an RNA-binding protein, which in turn helps restore normal mitophagy and blocks ferroptosis. This suggests a potential protective pathway that could be targeted to prevent anesthesia-related brain damage in young patients.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly examines mitophagy dysregulation in neurons as a mechanism of neurotoxicity, connecting to the project's core focus on mitophagy/autophagy pathways even though it centers on developmental anesthesia exposure rather than interneurons or spatial omics.

papers.title: Dihydromyricetin ameliorates cognitive dysfunction in SAMP8 mice via autophagy-mediated degradation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
papers.summary: This study looks at dihydromyricetin, a natural flavonoid compound, and tests whether it can improve cognitive decline in SAMP8 mice, a common model for accelerated brain aging. The researchers propose that the compound works by promoting autophagy, which then helps clear away the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein complex linked to neuroinflammation. The overall idea is that boosting autophagy reduces harmful inflammation in the brain, leading to better cognitive outcomes.
papers.why: This connects autophagy pathways to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline, relevant to understanding how autophagy-mediated clearance mechanisms in neurons could influence brain health and inform related mitophagy research.

papers.title: SIRT1 in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms, Disease Relevance, and Therapeutic Potential
papers.summary: This paper reviews the role of SIRT1, a NAD+-dependent deacetylase, in neurodegenerative diseases. It discusses the molecular pathways through which SIRT1 influences neuronal survival, protein aggregation, and cellular stress responses. The review also covers potential therapeutic strategies targeting SIRT1 to treat conditions like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
papers.why: SIRT1 is a known regulator of autophagy and mitophagy pathways in neurons, making its mechanisms directly relevant to understanding neurodegenerative processes tied to this project's focus on mitochondrial quality control in the brain.
